title: He Was Born in Delhi. He Delivered Parcels in Brisbane. Now He Could Play for Australia.
excerpt: India-born Nikhil Chaudhary has been called into Australia's T20I squad — the first India-born male cricketer selected since 1964.
body:
He was born in Delhi. He played 14 matches for Punjab between 2017 and 2019, sharing a dressing room with Harbhajan Singh and a teenaged Shubman Gill. He trialled with Mumbai Indians. None of it stuck.

In 2020, Nikhil Chaudhary flew to Queensland to visit an uncle. Then the pandemic shut Australia's borders. He stayed.

What followed was not the trajectory of a cricketer who knew he was destined for international cricket. He cut his finger working in a Mexican restaurant. He delivered parcels as a postman. He played grade cricket in Brisbane on weekends, the way thousands of migrants do — for love of the game, not because anyone was watching.

Someone was. James Hopes, the former Australian all-rounder coaching at Northern Suburbs, spotted Chaudhary and recommended him to the Hobart Hurricanes. By the 2024-25 Big Bash League season, Chaudhary was not just playing — he was instrumental in the Hurricanes' title win.

**On Wednesday, Cricket Australia named him in the T20I squad for the Bangladesh series.**

"Nikhil has been a player of national interest for some time," selector Tony Dodemaide said. "He was a standby player for this tour, joining the squad at pre-season camps in Brisbane, and comes in as a replacement for Travis Head."

If Chaudhary plays, he will become the first India-born male cricketer to represent Australia since Rex Sellers, a leg-spinner who made his only Test appearance in Kolkata in 1964. That is a 62-year wait.

**The numbers back the call.** In his most recent BBL season, Chaudhary scored 307 runs at a strike rate of 153, proving particularly devastating against pace — his strike rate against fast bowling hit 180. He made his Sheffield Shield debut for Tasmania and delivered immediately: a maiden first-class century against NSW and a five-wicket haul against Queensland in the same season. He is not an Australian citizen — he holds permanent residency — but fulfils the ICC's eligibility criteria.

There is a peculiar detail about Chaudhary that endears him to BBL crowds: his Kabaddi-inspired wicket celebrations, a nod to the sport he grew up playing in Delhi alongside cricket.

The 30-year-old's journey is not the standard migration story. He did not arrive on a cricket scholarship or through a state academy pathway. He arrived on a family visit, got stranded, and built a career from grade cricket pitches in Brisbane — a route that required more persistence than talent alone.

"He has also been part of the Delhi Capitals setup in this year's IPL," Dodemaide added. "Nikhil will gain invaluable experience in Bangladesh and will be in contention to play his first game for Australia when we sit down to pick a team for the opening T20 fixture."

**On the women's side**, Australia has already seen an India-born player thrive: Lisa Sthalekar represented Australia 187 times and captained the team. Chaudhary's call-up extends that tradition to the men's game, at a time when Australian cricket's diversity is broader than it has ever been.

For the Indian diaspora, Chaudhary's story is both specific and universal — a young cricketer from Delhi who found that the road to international cricket ran through a Brisbane grade ground, a pandemic border closure, and a Mexican restaurant kitchen.

nri_angle: Chaudhary's journey from Delhi domestic cricket to Australian international selection mirrors the broader diaspora experience of building a new life abroad, and his potential debut would end a 62-year wait for an India-born male cricketer in Australian colours.
